prize_parts.citation: For the discovery and development of halide perovskites as solution-processed light absorbers for high-efficiency solar cells

statement.case_for: Halide perovskites are a materials discovery in which crystal structure and composition explain function: the ABX3 framework, its soft ionic lattice and its defect tolerance account for the long carrier lifetimes and tunable band gaps. Efficiencies went from about 4 percent in Miyasaka's 2009 sensitized cell to certified values above 25 percent, reproduced independently in thousands of laboratories, and the structural chemistry has spread to LEDs, detectors and tandem devices. The opening ballots show real convergence on none of the candidates, so I judge on the strength of the chemistry. Here the structural evidence is solid: the phases, their transitions and their degradation products have been determined by diffraction and microscopy, not just inferred. Miyasaka (first perovskite-sensitized cell), Park (solid-state cell) and Snaith (meso-superstructured cell and rapid optimization) mark the three decisive steps that made the field.
statement.case_against: Credit is genuinely contested: Gratzel, Seok and Kanatzidis made major contributions, and any three-person cut leaves out serious people. Operational stability and lead toxicity are unresolved, so recognition may be early on technological maturity. A committee could also see the field as closer to physics or energy materials than to chemistry, and a prize built on device efficiency records is weaker than one built on a mechanistic or synthetic principle.

responses.point: Pd-catalyzed C-N coupling is a simple, general, industrially routine method that follows the 2010 cross-coupling tradition and is fully mature.
responses.response: I agree that B023 is mature and that its attribution to Buchwald and Hartwig is cleaner than the perovskite one. My reservation is conceptual novelty. The 2010 prize already recognized Pd cross-coupling as a principle, and C-N coupling is a very important extension of it with ligand design as the advance. I would hold B023 as a strong, safe candidate, but I do not think safety should outrank a new class of functional material. If the committee prefers a clean attribution, B023 is a defensible fallback, though not my first choice.

responses.point: B023 is the clearest case of a general method that changed how chemists build bonds; Kosugi's 1983 precedent is real but not general, and the decisive pair is Buchwald and Hartwig.
responses.response: I accept your attribution argument. Priority for a non-general stannylamine coupling should not displace the two who made it catalytic and general. Our difference is how to weigh extension against opening a field. You say perovskites have messy credit; I say that is true of most large fields, and Miyasaka, Park and Snaith still each have a documented, distinct first. Your point about overlap with 2010 is stronger than the credit question, and I would like colleagues to say whether it is disqualifying.

responses.point: Nanopore sequencing (B039) rests on a clear physical principle and delivered portable, label-free long-read sequencing, though allocation among Deamer, Branton, Bayley and Akeson is hard.
responses.response: I respect the enabling-technology argument, and it appeals to me as someone who values methods that let a community see what it could not see. But the credit problem is serious: Branton's and Bayley's status and the split between idea, pore engineering and enzyme ratchet cannot be resolved without a clear single contribution. Also, the chemistry here is mainly in the engineered protein pores and motor enzymes, while the central achievement is the sequencing platform. I rank it below B010 because the perovskite credit allocation is at least tractable and the structural chemistry is more central.

responses.point: Long-range electron transfer through proteins (B030) is a compact two-person credit with textbook-level confirmation and arguably late rather than premature recognition.
responses.response: The attribution to Gray and Winkler is the cleanest on the shortlist, and I agree it is late rather than early. My question is whether it is a discovery or the careful experimental validation of Marcus theory in proteins, which the committee already honored in 1992. I would ask what a citation would say that is not already covered. If you can state it in terms of new chemistry rather than confirmation of tunneling pathways, I would move it up.

responses.point: Biomolecular condensates (B052) are a new organizing principle for the cell, and are physical chemistry at heart.
responses.response: I take the conceptual argument seriously, but I am concerned about structural rigor. Many reported in vivo condensates are not demonstrated to be true phase-separated states rather than overexpression artefacts, and the molecular structure of the dense phase is poorly defined. You acknowledge that controversy yourself. Compared with perovskites, which have been certified and structurally characterized, I would wait until the field has settled what counts as a condensate before building a citation on it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept Miyasaka, Park and Snaith as the right three, given the claims of Gratzel, Seok and Kanatzidis.
Whether stability and lead toxicity make recognition early.
Whether B023 overlap with the 2010 prize is judged disqualifying or only a mild concern.
The first-place counts are spread thin, so no candidate has majority support yet.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. I am a Stockholm University colleague of Secretary Peter Brzezinski, but that is not a connection to any nominee. My own work on electron crystallography is adjacent to the structural characterization of porous and framework materials but not to perovskite photovoltaics.
